headline: Researchers used an IBM quantum processor to repeatedly measure and reset up to 100 qubits mid-calculation, a technique needed to keep future quantum computers reliable.
score_reason: Solid peer-reviewed physics result and a real step toward error correction, but the article says it is not a fault-tolerant machine.
importance_line: Researchers and quantum hardware makers gain evidence that today's chips can handle the repeated checking that error correction needs, though the demonstration is a physics experiment, not a working error-corrected computer.
summary: Interesting Engineering reports that a team from Rutgers University, IBM and other institutions, publishing in Nature Physics, ran nearly 5,000 two-qubit operations and almost 5,000 measure-and-reset cycles on a chain of up to 100 qubits of IBM's 156-qubit Heron processor. They found a sharp switch between chaotic and orderly behaviour, much like water freezing into ice, depending on how often qubits were measured and reset; the article stresses this does not yet make a fully fault-tolerant machine, meaning one that corrects its own errors reliably.
notes: Qubits are the basic units of a quantum computer. The Nature Physics paper itself was not read; facts come from the Interesting Engineering article.
